title: context Package
summary: `context.Context` carries **deadlines, cancellation signals, and request-scoped values** across API boundaries and goroutines. It's how a Go program says 'stop what you're doing' — when a client disconnects, a timeout fires, or a parent operation is abandoned — so work doesn't leak or run forever.

subtopics.title: What a Context carries
subtopics.explanation: A Context bundles three things: a Done() channel that closes when the operation should stop, an Err() that explains why it stopped (Canceled or DeadlineExceeded), and an optional Value(key) for request-scoped data. It's immutable — you derive new contexts from a parent rather than mutating one.

subtopics.title: Deriving contexts
subtopics.explanation: Start from context.Background() (top of a server) or context.TODO() (placeholder). Derive children with WithCancel, WithTimeout, WithDeadline, or WithValue. Cancelling or expiring a parent cancels all of its descendants, forming a cancellation tree.

subtopics.title: Always call cancel
subtopics.explanation: WithCancel/WithTimeout/WithDeadline return a cancel function that releases the context's resources (a timer and goroutine). You must call it — idiomatically `defer cancel()` — even after a normal finish, or you leak resources. go vet warns when you don't.
subtopics.example:
ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(parent, t)
defer cancel()

subtopics.title: Honoring cancellation
subtopics.explanation: Cancellation is cooperative: nothing is killed for you. Functions must select on ctx.Done() (or pass ctx to blocking calls like database/sql and net/http, which check it) and return promptly when it fires, propagating ctx.Err() up the stack.
subtopics.example: for { select { case <-ctx.Done(): return ctx.Err(); case j := <-jobs: do(j) } }

subtopics.title: Context values, used sparingly
subtopics.explanation: context.WithValue attaches request-scoped data (trace IDs, auth subject) keyed by an unexported custom type to avoid collisions. It is NOT for passing optional function parameters — values are untyped (any) and invisible in signatures. Keep it to cross-cutting metadata.
subtopics.example:
type ctxKey int
ctx = context.WithValue(ctx, traceKey, id)

subtopics.title: Context as the first parameter
subtopics.explanation: By convention ctx is the first argument of any function that does I/O or could block: func Do(ctx context.Context, ...). Never store a Context in a struct field — pass it explicitly down the call chain so cancellation flows correctly.
subtopics.example: func (s *Server) Handle(ctx context.Context, req Req) error

foundations.overview: In a server, a single request fans out into many goroutines — database queries, RPCs, cache lookups. If the client disconnects or the request times out, all that downstream work should stop immediately, not keep burning CPU and holding connections. context.Context is Go's standard mechanism for propagating that 'stop now' signal and a deadline across goroutine and API boundaries, plus carrying a little request-scoped metadata. It is woven through the standard library — net/http, database/sql, and most clients accept a Context as their first argument.
foundations.formalDefinition: context.Context is an interface providing a Done() channel that is closed when the context is cancelled or its deadline passes, an Err() reporting the cancellation cause, a Deadline(), and a Value(key) for request-scoped data. Contexts form an immutable tree where cancelling a parent cancels all descendants.
foundations.whyItMatters: Without context, goroutines spawned for a request leak when the request is abandoned, and slow downstream calls have no upper bound. Context gives every operation a deadline and a kill switch, which is essential for resilient services — and it's one of the most common Go interview and code-review topics.
foundations.mentalModel: Picture a manager (the request) handing out tasks to a team of workers (goroutines). Each worker gets a pager (the Context). When the manager cancels the project or the clock runs out, the manager pages everyone at once; good workers check their pager regularly and put down their tools. The Done() channel is the pager buzzing; Err() is the message explaining why.
foundations.runtimePerspective: A cancellable context is a small struct holding a Done channel and a children set. Cancellation closes the Done channel (a broadcast: every receiver unblocks) and recursively cancels children. WithTimeout adds a runtime timer that calls cancel when it fires. Selecting on ctx.Done() is just a channel receive that the scheduler wakes when the channel closes — cheap and integrated with goroutine parking.
foundations.realWorldUsage: net/http puts a per-request context on *http.Request (r.Context()) that's cancelled when the client disconnects; database/sql honors ctx to abort slow queries; gRPC propagates deadlines across service boundaries; pipelines pass ctx to every stage so the whole flow tears down together.
foundations.businessImpact: Deadlines bound tail latency and prevent one slow dependency from cascading into an outage; prompt cancellation frees connections and CPU under load, lowering infrastructure cost and improving reliability SLOs.
foundations.engineeringImpact: A consistent ctx-first convention makes cancellation and timeouts uniform across a codebase, so teams reason about shutdown and timeouts the same way everywhere and avoid goroutine leaks.
foundations.performanceImpact: Checking ctx.Done() is a cheap channel operation. The real win is bounding work: a request that would otherwise run 30 seconds against a dead client returns immediately, freeing resources. Forgetting to call cancel leaks a timer goroutine per call, which adds up.
commonUseCases: Per-request timeouts and cancellation in HTTP/gRPC servers
Aborting slow database queries and outbound calls
Graceful shutdown: cancel a root context to drain workers
Propagating trace IDs and auth identity as request-scoped values

commonMisconceptions.myth: Cancelling a context kills the goroutines using it.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Cancellation is cooperative — it only closes Done(). Code must check ctx.Done() and return; nothing is forcibly stopped.

commonMisconceptions.myth: context.WithValue is a general way to pass parameters.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It's for request-scoped cross-cutting metadata only. Values are untyped and hidden from signatures; pass real parameters explicitly.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You can skip calling cancel if the context finished normally.
commonMisconceptions.reality: You must always call cancel (defer it). Skipping it leaks the context's timer and bookkeeping until the parent is cancelled.

visualExplorer.title: How cancellation propagates
visualExplorer.caption: A timeout on a parent context fans out to every derived child and goroutine listening on Done().

config.intro: A request with a 2s timeout fans out to three workers. When the timeout fires:

steps.name: Derive the context
steps.detail: The handler calls ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(r.Context(), 2*time.Second) and defers cancel().

steps.name: Fan out
steps.detail: It launches workers, passing ctx to each. They do work and periodically select on ctx.Done().

steps.name: Deadline fires
steps.detail: After 2s the internal timer fires (or the client disconnects), and the context closes its Done() channel.

steps.name: Broadcast to children
steps.detail: Closing Done() unblocks every receiver at once, and the cancellation recurses into any child contexts.

steps.name: Workers exit & report
steps.detail: Each worker's select returns from <-ctx.Done(), it stops work and returns ctx.Err() (DeadlineExceeded), freeing connections.

interactiveExamples.title: A worker that respects cancellation
interactiveExamples.explanation: The worker loops, but each tick it also watches ctx.Done(). When the 100ms timeout fires, Done() closes, the select picks that case, and the worker returns ctx.Err() — context.DeadlineExceeded.

code.expectedOutput:
tick
tick
stopped: context deadline exceeded

interactiveExamples.title: Edit it: make the fetch cancellable
interactiveExamples.explanation: fetch ignores ctx, so it always sleeps the full 200ms even though the caller only allows 50ms. Edit fetch to return early via ctx.Done() so the deadline is honored.

checkpoints.code:
ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(context.Background())
cancel() // cancel immediately
<-ctx.Done()
err := ctx.Err()
fmt.Println(err)
checkpoints.explanation: Calling cancel() closes Done(), so the receive returns at once. ctx.Err() reports why it ended: context.Canceled, which prints as 'context canceled'. A timeout would instead give 'context deadline exceeded'.

checkpoints.prompt: What does cancelling a context actually do to the goroutines using it?
options: Closes the Done() channel so cooperating goroutines can choose to return
Pauses them until cancel is called again
checkpoints.explanation: Cancellation is cooperative. It closes Done(); goroutines must select on ctx.Done() and return themselves. Nothing is killed — code that never checks Done() keeps running.

checkpoints.prompt: What's wrong with this timeout usage?
options: The cancel function is discarded, leaking the context's timer until parent is cancelled
checkpoints.explanation: WithTimeout returns (ctx, cancel); discarding cancel with _ leaks the timer/goroutine the context allocated. Capture it and `defer cancel()`. go vet flags the lost cancel.

checkpoints.prompt: Complete the line so a slow query is aborted after 3 seconds and resources are released.
checkpoints.codeAfter:
defer cancel()
rows, err := db.QueryContext(ctx, query)
checkpoints.explanation: WithTimeout derives a child of the request context that is cancelled after 3s, and returns the cancel func we defer. QueryContext checks ctx and aborts the query when it fires.

codeLab.title: First successful result, or context error
codeLab.instructions: Implement `First(ctx, fns)` that runs each fn(ctx) in its own goroutine and returns the first value any of them produces. If ctx is cancelled/times out before any result arrives, return the zero value and ctx.Err(). Each fn returns (int, error); ignore fns that return an error.
hints: Use a buffered channel sized to len(fns) so a winning goroutine never blocks on send.
In each goroutine, only send when fn returns a nil error; otherwise just return.
In the outer select, race the results channel against ctx.Done() and return ctx.Err() if the context wins.

debuggingLab.title: A goroutine leak from an ignored context
debuggingLab.symptom: runtime.NumGoroutine() grows on every request; goroutines pile up blocked on a channel send.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: When ctx is cancelled, search returns -1 and stops receiving on out. But the spawned goroutine is still blocked on `out <- slowQuery()` with no receiver, so it leaks forever. The context cancelled the caller but not the orphaned sender.
commonMistakes: Using an unbuffered channel with a single receiver that might leave early.
Assuming context cancellation also unblocks goroutines that don't watch it.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Make the sender unable to block forever — buffer the channel (or have the goroutine also select on ctx.Done()).

theory.question: What three things does a context.Context carry, and how does cancellation work?
theory.directAnswer: It carries a Done() channel that closes when work should stop, an Err() explaining why it stopped (context.Canceled or context.DeadlineExceeded), and an optional Value(key) for request-scoped data. Cancellation is cooperative: cancelling or expiring a context closes Done(), and goroutines must select on ctx.Done() and return — nothing is forcibly killed. Cancelling a parent recursively cancels all derived child contexts.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: An interface for propagating deadlines, cancellation, and request-scoped values across goroutine and API boundaries.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To bound work and tear down goroutines when a request is abandoned or times out, preventing leaks and runaway latency.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Contexts form an immutable tree; closing Done() is a broadcast that unblocks all receivers, and cancellation recurses into children.

theory.whyImportant: Cancellation and deadlines are core to resilient services and a near-guaranteed Go interview topic.
theory.realWorldExample: An HTTP handler reads r.Context(); when the client disconnects that context is cancelled, so the database query started with QueryContext is aborted automatically.

followUps.question: Difference between context.Background() and context.TODO()?
followUps.answer: Both are non-cancellable roots; Background is the real top of a context tree, while TODO is a placeholder marking code that should later receive a real context.

followUps.question: Why must you always call the cancel function?
followUps.answer: WithCancel/WithTimeout allocate a timer and bookkeeping; cancel releases them. Skipping it leaks resources until the parent is cancelled, which go vet warns about.

theory.question: When should you use context.WithValue, and what are the pitfalls?
theory.directAnswer: Use WithValue only for request-scoped, cross-cutting metadata that travels with a request — trace IDs, auth subject, request IDs — not for passing ordinary function parameters. Pitfalls: values are untyped (any), so you lose compile-time safety and need type assertions; they're invisible in function signatures, hurting readability; and using a built-in type as the key risks collisions, so always key with an unexported custom type.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A derived context that attaches a single key/value pair for request-scoped data.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To thread cross-cutting metadata through call chains without adding it to every function signature.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Each WithValue wraps the parent; Value walks up the chain looking for a matching key, returning nil if absent.

theory.whyImportant: Misusing context values to pass real parameters is a common code-review red flag and a frequent interview probe.
theory.realWorldExample: Middleware extracts a trace ID from headers and stores it via WithValue so downstream logging can include it without changing every function's parameters.

followUps.question: Why use an unexported custom key type?
followUps.answer: It guarantees no other package can collide with your key, since the type itself is unexported and unique to your package.

followUps.question: Is context.Value lookup fast?
followUps.answer: It's a linear walk up the parent chain, so keep chains shallow and don't put hot-path data behind it.

scenario.question: Your API endpoint calls three downstream services sequentially. Under load, a single slow dependency makes the whole endpoint hang for 30 seconds and exhausts your connection pool. How do you use context to fix this?
scenario.directAnswer: Give the request an overall deadline with context.WithTimeout derived from r.Context(), and pass that ctx to every downstream call (they must use the *Context APIs like QueryContext / http.NewRequestWithContext). When the deadline fires, Done() closes, the in-flight call aborts and returns DeadlineExceeded, the handler returns an error instead of hanging, and the connection is released back to the pool. Optionally give each call its own sub-timeout. Always defer cancel().

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Bounding a request's total work with a propagated deadline.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: An unbounded downstream call ties up a goroutine and a pooled connection indefinitely, cascading into resource exhaustion.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The timeout context closes Done() at the deadline; ctx-aware clients abort their I/O and return ctx.Err(), freeing resources.

scenario.whyImportant: Unbounded downstream calls are a top cause of cascading outages; context deadlines are the standard mitigation.
scenario.realWorldExample: A checkout endpoint sets a 2s budget; when the inventory service is slow, the call aborts at 2s and the endpoint returns a degraded response rather than holding connections.

followUps.question: How do you split a total budget across calls?
followUps.answer: Derive a sub-context with a smaller WithTimeout (or compute remaining time from ctx.Deadline()) before each call, deferring each sub-cancel.

followUps.question: What if a downstream client ignores ctx?
followUps.answer: Then cancellation can't abort it; you must wrap it (e.g. select on ctx.Done() plus a result channel) or fix the client to accept a context.

coding.question: Implement `DoWithRetry(ctx, attempts, fn)` that retries fn up to `attempts` times with a fixed backoff, but stops immediately if ctx is cancelled. Return the last error if all attempts fail.
coding.thoughtProcess: Loop up to `attempts` times: call fn; on success return nil. On failure, sleep for the backoff but race that sleep against ctx.Done() using select so a cancellation aborts the wait instantly rather than after the full backoff. If ctx ends at any point, return ctx.Err().
coding.lineByLine: We track the latest error in err. Each iteration calls fn and returns nil on success. On the final attempt we break instead of sleeping. Otherwise the select waits for the backoff, but if ctx.Done() fires first we return ctx.Err() immediately — cancellation never has to wait out the full sleep. After the loop, err holds the last failure.
coding.timeComplexity: O(attempts) calls; wall-clock bounded by attempts*backoff or the context deadline, whichever is shorter.

followUps.question: How would you add exponential backoff?
followUps.answer: Compute the wait as base * 2^i (capped) and pass it to time.After, ideally with jitter to avoid thundering herds.

followUps.question: Why select on ctx.Done() during the sleep rather than just time.Sleep?
followUps.answer: time.Sleep ignores cancellation, so a cancelled request would still wait out the full backoff; the select aborts the wait the instant ctx is done.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Thread one request-scoped context from the server entry point down through every layer; pass it as the first parameter and never store it in a struct. Derive per-call timeouts from a single request budget so the whole tree shares one deadline.
productionDeepDive.performance: ctx.Done() checks are cheap channel ops; the payoff is bounding tail latency. Avoid putting hot-path data behind ctx.Value (it's a linear chain walk) and keep context trees shallow.
productionDeepDive.concurrency: Cancellation is the safe way to coordinate shutdown of many goroutines: cancel a root context and have every goroutine select on Done(). Combine with errgroup to cancel siblings when one fails.
productionDeepDive.reliability: Always set deadlines on outbound calls; an unbounded call is a latent outage. Ensure every spawned goroutine has a path to exit on cancellation, or you leak goroutines and connections.
productionDeepDive.observability: Carry a trace/request ID via WithValue so logs across goroutines correlate. Export NumGoroutine and alert on growth, and record how often calls end in DeadlineExceeded to spot failing dependencies.
productionDeepDive.security: Don't put secrets or large objects in context values; treat values as request metadata. Validate and re-derive deadlines at trust boundaries so a client can't request an unbounded operation.

caseStudies.problem: Work for disconnected clients kept running and holding resources.
caseStudies.solution: Each request carries a context (r.Context()) cancelled when the client disconnects; handlers and ctx-aware clients honor it.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Every layer must accept and respect ctx; legacy code that ignores it doesn't benefit.
caseStudies.lessons: Cancellation only works end-to-end if every layer threads the context through.

caseStudies.problem: Cross-service calls needed consistent timeouts and cancellation.
caseStudies.solution: Deadlines propagate in the context across service boundaries so a client timeout cancels server-side work.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Requires disciplined deadline budgeting across hops.
caseStudies.lessons: Propagated deadlines prevent one slow service from hanging an entire call chain.

keyTakeaways: A context carries a Done() cancellation channel, an Err() reason (Canceled or DeadlineExceeded), and optional request-scoped values; contexts form an immutable tree where cancelling a parent cancels all children.
Cancellation is cooperative — it only closes Done(); code must select on ctx.Done() and return. Nothing is forcibly killed.
Always derive timeouts with WithTimeout/WithCancel and defer cancel() to release resources; pass ctx as the first parameter and never store it in a struct.
Use context.WithValue only for request-scoped metadata keyed by an unexported type — never for ordinary parameters.
